aspectTitle: CSS visual-vs-DOM reorder: judging whether the source-order read still preserves meaning (F1 FAIL vs Example-2 PASS)
aspectDescription: A page uses CSS (absolute/relative positioning, flexbox order, flex-direction:row-reverse, grid-area/grid-template-areas) so the visual order differs from DOM source order. A tool can mechanically detect 'visual order != DOM order', but that mismatch is ONLY a 1.3.2 failure when reading the content in source order changes the MEANING. The SC pairs the explicit non-failure (Example 2: nav / main / side-story CSS-reordered, meaning unaffected = PASS) directly against the failure (F1 Products/Locations two-column example, where source order reads 'Products Locations Telephones Computers Portable
scenario: SaaS two-plan pricing comparison built from position:absolute chips. Plans authored low-to-high (Starter, Growth); the two price chips emitted in REVERSE source order ($79 first, then $19). CSS coordinates land each price in the correct visual column, but linearized the page reads 'Starter ... Growth ... $79 ... $19', binding the expensive price to the cheaper plan and swapping the prices relative to source.
mechanism: position:absolute on every .plan and .price; the .price chips' DOM order is the reverse of the .plan cards' DOM order (F1 archetype), so the programmatically-determined reading sequence binds each price to the wrong plan.

scenario: Recipe blog 'Brown-Butter Madeleines' with a four-step Method as a real <ol>. flex-direction:row-reverse + flex-wrap:wrap-reverse renders the cards 1,2,3,4 top-to-bottom while the <ol> source order is 4,3,2,1. Because an ordered list is an inherently meaningful sequence, a screen reader announces 'item 1 of 4' on the BAKE step, linearizing the recipe into a dangerous order (bake the batter before mixing it).

aspectTitle: Layout-table linearization that scrambles a meaningful sequence (F49) — reading 2-D content as a linear story
aspectDescription: An HTML <table> used purely for layout (WCAG explicitly permits layout tables) presents content that reads correctly in two visual dimensions, but when linearized row-by-row, cell-by-cell, the meaningful sequence breaks. F49's two canonical cases: (1) the advertisement where a rowspan stitches 'XYZ mountaineering top!' into one line and separates it from 'XYZ gets you to the', destroying the slogan 'XYZ gets you to the top!'; (2) the museum page where left-column nav links are interleaved with the right-column image/placard/heading/description, so the description is shredded by Link 2, Link 3,
scenario: Mountaineering-retailer promo banner built as a layout table: a wordmark cell and a giant italic 'top!' in a rowspan=2 bottom-aligned cell visually finish the slogan in the row below ('Summit Provisions gets you to the top!'), but the rowspan places 'top!' before the clause in source order. This is F49's canonical advertisement case.
mechanism: A rowspan=2 cell reorders the content stream so the punch word 'top!' is read before the clause it completes; linearized DOM order (verified via Puppeteer) is 'Summit Provisions Mountaineering Outfitters | top! | Summit Provisions gets you to the', splitting the slogan that is a meaningful sequence.

scenario: Boutique yoga studio hero headline reads 'W E L C O M E', built by inserting   between every letter of the single word 'Welcome' (F32 FAIL), on the same page as a primary-nav 'FAQ' link visually tracked the correct way with CSS letter-spacing (initialism carve-out, PASS). aspectTitle: Faked columns / faked tables in pre-formatted plain text (F33, F34): visual 2-D structure with zero DOM structure
aspectDescription: Content is laid out with literal space/tab/line-break characters inside a <pre>, <textarea>, code block, or monospaced <div>, faking multiple newspaper columns (F33) or a data table (F34, the Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner menu). Visually it looks like two columns or a grid; in the linear character stream a screen reader reads ACROSS the fake columns, interleaving them into gibberish (e.g. 'Web Content Accessibility Guidelines including blindness and low vision'). There is NO table/column markup at all — so the only signal is that the rendered visual implies a 2-D structure the linear character stream
scenario: Desktop-software EULA install screen renders the license body as a single monospaced <pre> inside a focusable scroll region. To fit the page, two unrelated clauses are laid out as newspaper columns with padding spaces: each source line holds a fragment of the LEFT clause, a space gutter, then a fragment of a DIFFERENT RIGHT clause. Sighted users read each column top-to-bottom; AT reads each line across, splicing the grant clause into the middle of the reverse-engineering/transfer restriction clause.
mechanism: F33 — white-space characters create two columns in plain text. The column relationship exists only as space padding inside one <pre> (no <table>, no CSS column-count). A screen reader reads the character stream in line order, so the first spoken line becomes '1. GRANT OF LICENSE. Aperture Software grants and may not be reverse engineered,' — clause 1's opening fused onto the restriction clause's middle. No correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined, so the legalese the user must accept is unintelligible.

scenario: An independent diner's 'This Week's Specials' chalkboard panel presents a genuine data table — rows are weekday ranges (Mon-Tue/Wed-Thu/Fri-Sat), columns are Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner, cells hold a dish plus a price — laid out entirely with space characters in one monospaced <pre>. The header row, the weekday row labels, and the price sub-columns are implied only by alignment. No <table>, <th>, scope, headers, or role exists.
mechanism: F34 — white space formats a table in plain text. Header cells cannot be associated with data cells and the linear read glues unrelated cells together: the first data line is announced 'Mon-Tue Buttermilk stack French dip $12 Meatloaf $15' (three different meals + two prices fused), exactly the F34 'Monday 2 fried eggs tomato soup garden salad' shape. Continuation lines detach sides/prices from their dish, and 'Breakfast Lunch Dinner' is read once with no tie to any cell.

scenario: A self-service 'Team Email Signature' tool outputs a ready-to-paste signature in a read-only <textarea>. The signature is a directory card whose rows align three columns — Name | Title | Phone — using literal TAB characters (tab-size:12, monospace). Rendered, it is a tidy 3-column staff roster; the columns are carried entirely by tab stops, with no <table>, list, or role.
mechanism: F33/F34 family applied to tabs. Screen readers do not announce tab stops as column boundaries, so AT reads each row as one run — 'Dr. Amara Osei Medical Director x4120 / 555-0142' — with the tab stops collapsed away. Because every row repeats the pattern and names contain spaces, the listener cannot reliably tell where a name ends and a title begins, or which extension pairs with which person. The Name->Title->Phone relationship the layout promises is destroyed on linearization.

aspectTitle: Faked columns / faked tables in pre-formatted plain text (F33, F34): visual 2-D structure with zero DOM structure
aspectDescription: Content is laid out with literal space/tab/line-break characters inside a <pre>, <textarea>, code block, or monospaced <div>, faking multiple newspaper columns (F33) or a data table (F34, the Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner menu). Visually it looks like two columns or a grid; in the linear character stream a screen reader reads ACROSS the fake columns, interleaving them into gibberish (e.g. 'Web Content Accessibility Guidelines including blindness and low vision'). There is NO table/column markup at all — so the only signal is that the rendered visual implies a 2-D structure the linear character stream
scenario: A 'Your trip is confirmed' airline page shows the itinerary in a read-only <textarea>. The block is a six-column data table — Flight | Date | Route | Depart | Arrive | Gate — aligned with space characters in a monospace font, mimicking the confirmation grids airlines email. The safety-relevant Gate cell sits in the rightmost space-aligned column; alignment alone encodes which value belongs to which field and row. No <table>, role, or list.

With every row repeating times and a short gate token, the listener must hold six fields in working memory and infer the trailing token is the gate, but the unassociated header row anchors nothing — so the gate detaches from its flight, defeating exactly what the traveler most needs.

scenario: A user-submitted guitar chord chart for 'Harbor Lights' uses the universal chords-above-lyrics convention: a chord line and a lyric line alternate, and each chord is padded with leading spaces so that, in a monospace font, it sits directly ABOVE the exact syllable where the chord change happens. aspectTitle: Bidirectional / mixed-directionality text where the visual order is fixed by reordering characters, exposing the wrong order to AT (G57 bidi case)

The correct fix is markup (dir, <bdi>, <bdo>) that overrides the bidi algorithm so the order is right both visually AND to AT, NOT reordering source characters. Conversely, omitting
scenario: Arabic (RTL) dates-store product price line. The price '$50' plus its sentence period were physically moved to the FRONT of the source byte stream ('.$50 سعر العلبة الواحدة …') so the bidirectional algorithm mirrors them and the screen shows a clean '… $50.' at the visual left end. Verified with a rendering harness: LOGICAL source order is '.$50 سعر…' (price/period first) while VISUAL is '…سعر العلبة الواحدة $50.'
mechanism: G57 source-character reordering: punctuation + an embedded LTR price run relocated in the content stream to satisfy the bidi algorithm, so a screen reader/Braille/copy-paste reads the period and price FIRST, detached from the Arabic clause — the wrong logical order — while the render looks correct. Fix would be <bdi>$50</bdi> with the period in logical final position.

aspectDescription: 1.3.2 only applies 'when the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning,' and the Understanding adds three clarifications: providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning; there may be more than one 'correct' order; only one correct order needs to be provided. Two independent non-interleaved articles, a nav-vs-main pairing, and a magazine article with callout sidebars can each appear in EITHER order without failing — the container has no meaningful sequence even though each article does. The evaluator must first decide whether order is meaningful f
scenario: Naturalists' bulletin with two fully independent, non-interleaved articles in a two-column flex layout. The visually dominant photo-led feature ('Return of the curlew') is in the right column but is DOM-second; the short treasurer's notice is DOM-first. Neither article is reordered internally and they are not interleaved, so the container has no meaningful sequence and either order is correct.
mechanism: A screen reader reads the notice in full then the feature in full, each in clean source order and internally coherent, with nothing interleaved. Because the two articles are semantically independent, hearing one before the other does not change either's meaning — the container is order-irrelevant (the Understanding's 'two independent articles' case). The applicability gate is not tripped.

aspectTitle: Applicability gate and multiple-valid-orders: deciding whether order is meaningful at all, and that more than one order can be correct
aspectDescription: 1.3.2 only applies 'when the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning,' and the Understanding adds three clarifications: providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning; there may be more than one 'correct' order; only one correct order needs to be provided. Two independent non-interleaved articles, a nav-vs-main pairing, and a magazine article with callout sidebars can each appear in EITHER order without failing — the container has no meaningful sequence even though each article does. The evaluator must first decide whether order is meaningful f
scenario: Saved bank support-chat transcript (a duplicate-charge dispute). Each bubble is a CSS-grid item, and grid-row lays them out in the correct visual conversation order; but the DOM stores messages newest-first (a 'prepend new message' anti-pattern), so the linearized reading order is the exact reverse — the agent's closing 'Glad I could help! The refund will land in 3-5 working days' is read before the customer's opening 'Hi, I was charged twice...'.
mechanism: A screen reader and the linearized DOM ignore grid-row and read source order m6→m1: the resolution is announced before the problem and every answer before its question. A non-sighted user cannot follow the dispute. A conversation is intrinsically meaningful sequence (a reply only makes sense after the message it answers), and the programmatically determined order contradicts it.
